screens.title: Advanced SD-WAN Features and Integration
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll explore the advanced features of Cisco SD‑WAN that matter most for cloud-first organizations. You will learn what Direct Internet Access means for branch performance, how Cloud OnRamp optimizes SaaS and IaaS connectivity, and how security services integrate with the fabric through local inspection or service chaining. We’ll also cover multicast, advanced QoS across the overlay, and how to make controllers highly available. Each concept includes practical configuration patterns and common mistakes to avoid. For example, you’ll see why breaking out traffic locally improves Office 365 performance but requires careful security steering, and how Cloud OnRamp uses real‑time telemetry and application-aware routing to pick the best internet path for a SaaS flow. By the end of the chapter you should be able to explain tradeoffs for local breakout versus backhaul, design basic Cloud OnRamp attachments to a public cloud, and plan controller redundancy so the SD‑WAN fabric remains operational during failures. Consider how delivering security closer to the user changes your testing approach and what verification commands you would run after deployment.

screens.title: Direct Internet Access (DIA) — Why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Direct Internet Access lets branches send internet‑bound traffic straight to the internet instead of backhauling all traffic through a central data center. The key claim is simple: reducing path length improves latency and user experience for cloud and SaaS applications. As an example, Office 365 traffic that would otherwise travel from the branch to the data center and then out to the internet sees fewer hops and less delay when broken out locally to the branch's internet TLOC. That said, DIA is not just a performance decision: it requires a policy and security design. A misconception is thinking DIA is safe by default; without local firewalling or cloud security inspection, branches are exposed. In Cisco SD‑WAN, the fabric uses centralized data policies to identify internet flows and instruct the edge to prefer a local internet TLOC. You should be able to explain the two common implementations: a local breakout where the edge performs NAT and forwards directly, or a cloud security integration where the edge steers traffic to a cloud gateway for inspection first. Practical takeaway: plan both policy-based steering and security inspection before enabling DIA so performance gains do not compromise protection. How would you validate that traffic is actually breaking out locally in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DIA enables branch offices to break out internet traffic locally to improve SaaS performance, requiring policy steering and security controls.

content.html:
Core Concept
Direct Internet Access (DIA)
Local breakout for better SaaS performance, with security and policy tradeoffs.
What DIA is
Branches forward internet-bound flows to a local internet TLOC instead of backhauling. This reduces latency and conserves data center bandwidth.
Local breakout: edge NAT and direct internet forward.
Cloud security integration: steer flows to a cloud gateway for inspection before exit.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

DIA improves cloud app performance but must be paired with local or cloud inspection to maintain security.

Practical example
If Office 365 users in a branch report slow mail or OneDrive access, enabling DIA for Office 365 flows and steering to the best internet TLOC often reduces latency and improves experience.
Common mistake
Enabling DIA without firewall/IPS or cloud inspection exposes branches to direct internet threats.
Check your understanding
Name one verification command you would use on a cEdge to confirm DIA NAT is active and one policy check to confirm the fabric is steering Office 365 to the local TLOC.

screens.title: DIA Implementation — Policy and NAT
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing DIA in Cisco SD‑WAN combines a centralized routing decision with local device configuration. The core flow is: identify internet-bound traffic centrally, push a data policy that sets the preferred TLOC color to the branch's internet link, and ensure the edge has NAT configured so private addresses can egress. For example, you create a centralized data policy that matches VPN 10 source networks and destination prefix 0.0.0.0/0, and the action sets the tloc-action to the business internet color. The misconception to avoid is believing the policy alone makes breakout possible; NAT and interface configuration on the cEdge are required so the return path works and translations appear in show output. When you deploy this, verify with show ip nat translations and check the data policy application status in vManage. Also test from a real host in the VPN to confirm public IP assignment and that the traffic path matches the expected TLOC. In practice, coordinate apply timing: enable NAT after policy is staged to avoid temporary black‑holing, and include a default action in the policy to accept non-matched traffic. What verification steps will you script for rollout to multiple branches?

keyIdea.title: Implementation pattern
keyIdea.text: Centralized data policy selects the local internet TLOC; cEdge NAT enables address translation and correct return paths for DIA.

content.html:
Process Flow
DIA Implementation: Policy + NAT
Step-by-step
1.
Define a prefix list for internet destinations (0.0.0.0/0) in vManage and include it in a data policy.
2.
Create a site and VPN list that targets the branch VPN from which you want breakout.
3.
In the data policy rule, match source VPN and destination prefix list, then set the tloc-action to the branch 'biz-internet' color.
4.
Configure NAT on the cEdge interface in VPN 0 and mark inside on VPN 10 so translations occur.
Verification and tips
  • On the cEdge: check show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics after test traffic.
  • In vManage: confirm the policy is pushed and the site list/vpn list match the branch.
  • Staging tip: enable policy then NAT in a controlled window to prevent transient black holes.
Common mistake
Relying on policy without configuring NAT or proper interface directions will cause return traffic failures.

screens.title: Configure DIA: cEdge NAT CLI Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows the exact CLI pattern you use on a cEdge to implement NAT for a VPN that will break out locally. Start by defining an access list that identifies the VPN's internal subnet as interesting traffic. Then configure the internet-facing interface in VPN 0 as ip nat outside, mark the internal VPN as ip nat inside, and configure an overload NAT rule that uses the interface address for translation. The concrete code block shows a common configuration. A common misconception is that NAT commands alone are sufficient; remember you must also create and apply the centralized data policy in vManage so the fabric steers matching traffic to the local internet TLOC. After applying the CLI, verify with show ip nat translations and simulate traffic from a host in the VPN to confirm translations and connectivity. When you deploy to multiple branches, convert these commands into a template or automation job and validate one site before broad rollout. What monitoring checks will you include to detect NAT exhaustion or translation failures? Configure DIA: cEdge NAT CLI Walkthrough means configure access-list to match vpn host subnets, mark interfaces inside/outside for nat, and apply overload to the biz-internet interface.. In practical terms, example cli commands to enable nat overload for vpn breakout. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Hands-on
cEdge NAT example
This CLI config enables PAT for VPN 10 using the gigabit interface connected to biz-internet.
! On the cEdge router CLI
! Define interesting traffic from VPN 10
ip access-list extended VPN10_TO_INTERNET
 permit ip 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any
!
! Configure NAT on the VPN 0 interface connected to biz-internet
vpn 0
 interface GigabitEthernet0/2  ! Assuming this is your biz-internet interface
  ip nat outside
 exit
!
vpn 10
 ip nat inside
 ip nat inside source list VPN10_TO_INTERNET interface GigabitEthernet0/2 overload
!
! Verify NAT configuration
! show ip nat translations
! show ip nat statistics
Scenario
Branch with single public IP; use PAT to allow many hosts to egress via the interface address.
Verification
Confirm active translations and test web access from a host in VPN 10; check vManage for policy push status.

screens.title: Cloud OnRamp for SaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud OnRamp for SaaS monitors performance to SaaS endpoints and uses that telemetry to choose the best internet path from a branch. The central claim is that real‑time metrics like latency, loss, and jitter let SD‑WAN pick the best TLOC for an application, improving user experience without manual path selection. For example, vEdge or cEdge routers can measure paths to Office 365 endpoints and, via application identification and application-aware routing, steer traffic over the internet link with the best observed performance. A common misconception is that Cloud OnRamp magically accelerates SaaS — in reality it chooses the best existing path and requires accurate application identification and properly defined AAR policies. In practice you must define SLA thresholds and maintain accurate application lists. For validation, observe AAR decisions in vManage and confirm that when a link degrades, the fabric shifts Office 365 flows to a healthier internet TLOC. Takeaway: Cloud OnRamp reduces manual tuning by automating path selection, but you must verify application identification and SLA settings to avoid traffic blackholing. In practical terms, using telemetry and aar to optimize saas paths. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept
Cloud OnRamp for SaaS
Telemetry-driven path selection using Application-Aware Routing.
How it works
Routers measure path health to SaaS endpoints and vManage applies AAR policies to steer flows to the best TLOC.
Example
If the primary ISP shows increased loss to Office 365, AAR can move that traffic to the secondary ISP with better measured metrics.
Common mistake
Incorrect application lists or SLA thresholds can cause misclassification or traffic black‑holing.
Validation
Observe AAR decisions in vManage and run synthetic tests to SaaS endpoints while toggling link characteristics to confirm automatic failover.

screens.title: Cloud OnRamp for IaaS
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud OnRamp for IaaS creates a secure, policy-driven extension of your SD‑WAN fabric into public clouds by deploying virtual cEdge routers inside the provider VPC or VNet. The central idea is that the virtual cEdge forms IPsec tunnels back to on‑premises edges and participates in OMP, so cloud workloads appear as part of the enterprise WAN. For example, you can deploy a virtual cEdge in an Azure VNet and configure it to establish IPsec to your branch cEdges and data center. Misconceptions include thinking this is purely a connectivity template — you must plan subnets, security groups, and route exchange carefully. Control plane integration means policies applied centrally are enforced across cloud and on‑prem endpoints, enabling consistent security and QoS. Operational checks include verifying IPsec tunnel status, OMP route exchange to ensure cloud prefixes appear in the fabric, and testing traffic paths to confirm proper steering and performance. The takeaway: Cloud OnRamp for IaaS simplifies cloud extension but requires cloud-specific deployment and security planning to succeed. Cloud OnRamp for IaaS means deploy virtual cedge in cloud vpcs/vnets and form ipsec tunnels so the cloud region becomes a native part of the sd‑wan fabric.. In practical terms, extending the sd‑wan fabric into public clouds with virtual cedge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architecture
Cloud OnRamp for IaaS
Virtual cEdge deployment inside public cloud to extend the SD‑WAN fabric.
Key components
  • Virtual cEdge in the VPC/VNet
  • IPsec tunnels between cloud cEdge and on‑prem edges
  • OMP route exchange for prefix distribution
Operational checklist
Verify cloud security group rules, ensure IPsec tunnels are established, confirm OMP routes for cloud prefixes, and test application connectivity from on‑prem to cloud workloads.
Example
A web front end in a cloud VPC uses a virtual cEdge to announce its prefix, making it routable from branches with consistent data policies.
Common mistake
Omitting cloud-side firewall and IAM considerations leads to unreachable services or insecure exposure despite a functioning tunnel.

screens.title: Security Integration and Service Chaining
screens.narratorSegment: Security integration in Cisco SD‑WAN spans running services locally on edge routers and steering flows to external security gateways. Edge devices can host stateful firewall, IPS, and URL filtering to inspect traffic before it leaves the branch. Service chaining lets you direct traffic to a physical or virtual appliance or to a cloud security gateway like Umbrella for advanced inspection. A concrete scenario: you want all web traffic inspected by a cloud SWG even when using DIA. You create a centralized data policy that matches HTTP/HTTPS and sets a service action to redirect those flows to the cloud security gateway. A common misconception is thinking service chaining adds no latency; in fact it adds processing and possibly a detour, so include SLA objectives in design and monitor path health. Validation steps include confirming the policy push, monitoring tunnels to the security service, and testing that inspected traffic receives expected blocking or logging. Key takeaway: integrate security into DIA and Cloud OnRamp designs to prevent opening attack surface when breaking out locally. Security Integration and Service Chaining means combine local edge services and service chaining to cloud security gateways so dia and cloud onramp do not bypass inspection.. In practical terms, local inspection, edge services, and steering to cloud gateways. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Security Integration & Service Chaining
Ensure DIA and Cloud OnRamp traffic are inspected by local or cloud security services.
Local services

screens.narratorSegment: Service chaining is implemented through centralized data policies that match traffic and set a service action instead of simply setting a preferred TLOC. The pattern is: define the service (cloud security gateway or appliance) in vManage, create match conditions that identify the traffic to inspect, and set the action to forward that traffic to the service. Also watch for latency or throughput impacts, and include fallback rules in the policy to accept or send traffic via a default path if the service becomes unreachable. screens.title: Multicast Support in SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: Multicast over SD‑WAN is challenging because the overlay uses unicast IPsec tunnels by default. The solution is to enable multicast routing inside the VPNs and let the control plane distribute multicast information. Concretely, you enable PIM on service‑side interfaces and enable multicast routing on the relevant VPNs. The vSmart controller distributes multicast routing information such as Rendezvous Points (RPs) and sources via OMP so edge routers know where to forward multicast. Edge devices then encapsulate multicast as unicast IPsec packets and replicate them to interested receivers across the overlay. A common misconception is assuming multicast will flow without PIM or OMP configuration; without those, multicast is not replicated and receivers will not get traffic. In practice, plan RP discovery, verify PIM neighbor relationships on service interfaces, and check OMP multicast route propagation. For example, a live video stream from a data center multicast source will reach branch receivers only when PIM is active at the service interfaces and multicast is enabled in the VPN. The key takeaway: multicast requires deliberate control‑plane and data‑plane configuration when carried over an SD‑WAN overlay.

screens.title: Advanced QoS in SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: Advanced QoS in SD‑WAN combines local queue configuration with centralized policy actions so traffic receives consistent treatment across the overlay. The claim is that classification and marking must be enforced both at the edge and respected by intermediate links. For example, you can classify an ERP application by its application ID or DSCP and map it to a high‑priority queue in the edge then re‑mark DSCP values as traffic traverses the overlay. A common misconception is assuming DSCP values will always survive the overlay; the fabric can re‑mark values to enforce consistent treatment, but this must be explicitly configured. Use centralized data policies to classify traffic and map to QoS queues, and ensure per-interface queueing and policing are present on the edge device. Verify by generating traffic that mimics real application load and checking queue counters and DSCP markings at each hop. Practical takeaway: blend centralized classification with device-level queue configuration to guarantee performance for critical apps even over congested internet transports. screens.title: Controller High Availability (HA)
screens.narratorSegment: Controller HA is a requirement, not an option, for resilient SD‑WAN operations. vManage typically runs as a cluster for management-plane continuity; a three-node or larger cluster ensures that management functions survive individual node failures. vSmart controllers are often deployed in active/active mode so OMP control plane load is distributed and edges can peer to multiple vSmarts for redundancy. vBond orchestrators are also deployed in multiples so onboarding continues if a single orchestrator fails. A common misconception is believing that edge devices need only one controller address — in reality, edges are configured with a list of controller IPs so they can failover. Operational considerations include synchronizing configuration and certificates across clustered vManage nodes, confirming that edges establish OMP peering to available vSmarts, and scripting failover tests to validate behavior. For example, simulate a vSmart failure and confirm OMP routes are still exchanged via remaining vSmarts and that traffic forwarding continues without fabric-wide outages. The essential design insight: reduce single points of failure by deploying multiple controllers with clear peering and certificate management. Controller High Availability (HA) means deploy vmanage clusters, multiple vsmart controllers, and multiple vbonds to avoid single points of failure; validate peering and failover behavior.. Controller High Availability
Design vManage, vSmart, and vBond for redundancy to keep management and control planes available under failure.

Cluster multiple vManage nodes for management continuity and configuration consistency.

Deploy multiple vSmarts active/active so edges peer with more than one controller for OMP control plane redundancy.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore the advanced features of Cisco SD‑WAN that matter most for cloud-first organizations. You will learn what Direct Internet Access means for branch performance, how Cloud OnRamp optimizes SaaS and IaaS connectivity, and how security services integrate with the fabric through local inspection or service chaining. We’ll also cover multicast, advanced QoS across the overlay, and how to make controllers highly available. Each concept includes practical configuration patterns and common mistakes to avoid. For example, you’ll see why breaking out traffic locally improves Office 365 performance but requires careful security steering, and how Cloud OnRamp uses real‑time telemetry and application-aware routing to pick the best internet path for a SaaS flow. By the end of the chapter you should be able to explain tradeoffs for local breakout versus backhaul, design basic Cloud OnRamp attachments to a public cloud, and plan controller redundancy so the SD‑WAN fabric remains operational during failures. Consider how delivering security closer to the user changes your testing approach and what verification commands you would run after deployment.

This chapter has focused learning objectives you should master. First, you will explain Direct Internet Access: why branches break out locally and how centralized data policies and local NAT enable safe, high‑performing breakouts. Second, you’ll describe Cloud OnRamp for SaaS and IaaS, including how telemetry and virtual cEdge routers extend the fabric into public clouds. Third, you will understand how to integrate security — from local stateful firewall and IPS on edge devices to service chaining that directs traffic to cloud security gateways. Fourth, you will explore multicast support in the SD‑WAN overlay, learning why PIM and OMP cooperation is necessary to carry multicast across unicast IPsec tunnels. Each objective is practical: you will see configuration patterns, verification steps, and common mistakes to avoid so you can both design and troubleshoot these features in production.

First, you will understand multicast support: how PIM and OMP work together so multicast can traverse IPsec overlays and what configuration steps are required. Second, you will learn advanced QoS across SD‑WAN: classification, DSCP mapping and re‑marking, and applying end‑to‑end policies so critical apps keep priority. Third, plan high availability for controllers: how vManage clustering, multiple vSmart controllers, and multiple vBond orchestrators prevent single points of failure. Fourth, you will identify common mistakes — from insecure DIA deployments to misconfigured Cloud OnRamp policies — and learn validation checks to avoid them. You should be able to validate NAT translations, verify AAR path selection, confirm PIM neighbor relationships, and test controller failover behavior. Direct Internet Access lets branches send internet‑bound traffic straight to the internet instead of backhauling all traffic through a central data center. The key claim is simple: reducing path length improves latency and user experience for cloud and SaaS applications. As an example, Office 365 traffic that would otherwise travel from the branch to the data center and then out to the internet sees fewer hops and less delay when broken out locally to the branch's internet TLOC. That said, DIA is not just a performance decision: it requires a policy and security design. A misconception is thinking DIA is safe by default; without local firewalling or cloud security inspection, branches are exposed. In Cisco SD‑WAN, the fabric uses centralized data policies to identify internet flows and instruct the edge to prefer a local internet TLOC. You should be able to explain the two common implementations: a local breakout where the edge performs NAT and forwards directly, or a cloud security integration where the edge steers traffic to a cloud gateway for inspection first. Practical takeaway: plan both policy-based steering and security inspection before enabling DIA so performance gains do not compromise protection. How would you validate that traffic is actually breaking out locally in your environment?

Implementing DIA in Cisco SD‑WAN combines a centralized routing decision with local device configuration. The core flow is: identify internet-bound traffic centrally, push a data policy that sets the preferred TLOC color to the branch's internet link, and ensure the edge has NAT configured so private addresses can egress. For example, you create a centralized data policy that matches VPN 10 source networks and destination prefix 0.0.0.0/0, and the action sets the tloc-action to the business internet color. The misconception to avoid is believing the policy alone makes breakout possible; NAT and interface configuration on the cEdge are required so the return path works and translations appear in show output. When you deploy this, verify with show ip nat translations and check the data policy application status in vManage. Also test from a real host in the VPN to confirm public IP assignment and that the traffic path matches the expected TLOC. In practice, coordinate apply timing: enable NAT after policy is staged to avoid temporary black‑holing, and include a default action in the policy to accept non-matched traffic. What verification steps will you script for rollout to multiple branches?

This walkthrough shows the exact CLI pattern you use on a cEdge to implement NAT for a VPN that will break out locally. Start by defining an access list that identifies the VPN's internal subnet as interesting traffic. Then configure the internet-facing interface in VPN 0 as ip nat outside, mark the internal VPN as ip nat inside, and configure an overload NAT rule that uses the interface address for translation. The concrete code block shows a common configuration. A common misconception is that NAT commands alone are sufficient; remember you must also create and apply the centralized data policy in vManage so the fabric steers matching traffic to the local internet TLOC. After applying the CLI, verify with show ip nat translations and simulate traffic from a host in the VPN to confirm translations and connectivity. When you deploy to multiple branches, convert these commands into a template or automation job and validate one site before broad rollout. The central claim is that real‑time metrics like latency, loss, and jitter let SD‑WAN pick the best TLOC for an application, improving user experience without manual path selection. For example, vEdge or cEdge routers can measure paths to Office 365 endpoints and, via application identification and application-aware routing, steer traffic over the internet link with the best observed performance. Multicast over SD‑WAN is challenging because the overlay uses unicast IPsec tunnels by default. The solution is to enable multicast routing inside the VPNs and let the control plane distribute multicast information. Concretely, you enable PIM on service‑side interfaces and enable multicast routing on the relevant VPNs. The vSmart controller distributes multicast routing information such as Rendezvous Points (RPs) and sources via OMP so edge routers know where to forward multicast. Edge devices then encapsulate multicast as unicast IPsec packets and replicate them to interested receivers across the overlay. A common misconception is assuming multicast will flow without PIM or OMP configuration; without those, multicast is not replicated and receivers will not get traffic. In practice, plan RP discovery, verify PIM neighbor relationships on service interfaces, and check OMP multicast route propagation. For example, a live video stream from a data center multicast source will reach branch receivers only when PIM is active at the service interfaces and multicast is enabled in the VPN. The key takeaway: multicast requires deliberate control‑plane and data‑plane configuration when carried over an SD‑WAN overlay.

Advanced QoS in SD‑WAN combines local queue configuration with centralized policy actions so traffic receives consistent treatment across the overlay. The claim is that classification and marking must be enforced both at the edge and respected by intermediate links. For example, you can classify an ERP application by its application ID or DSCP and map it to a high‑priority queue in the edge then re‑mark DSCP values as traffic traverses the overlay. A common misconception is assuming DSCP values will always survive the overlay; the fabric can re‑mark values to enforce consistent treatment, but this must be explicitly configured. Use centralized data policies to classify traffic and map to QoS queues, and ensure per-interface queueing and policing are present on the edge device. Verify by generating traffic that mimics real application load and checking queue counters and DSCP markings at each hop. Practical takeaway: blend centralized classification with device-level queue configuration to guarantee performance for critical apps even over congested internet transports. Controller HA is a requirement, not an option, for resilient SD‑WAN operations. vManage typically runs as a cluster for management-plane continuity; a three-node or larger cluster ensures that management functions survive individual node failures. vSmart controllers are often deployed in active/active mode so OMP control plane load is distributed and edges can peer to multiple vSmarts for redundancy. vBond orchestrators are also deployed in multiples so onboarding continues if a single orchestrator fails. A common misconception is believing that edge devices need only one controller address — in reality, edges are configured with a list of controller IPs so they can failover. Operational considerations include synchronizing configuration and certificates across clustered vManage nodes, confirming that edges establish OMP peering to available vSmarts, and scripting failover tests to validate behavior. For example, simulate a vSmart failure and confirm OMP routes are still exchanged via remaining vSmarts and that traffic forwarding continues without fabric-wide outages. The essential design insight: reduce single points of failure by deploying multiple controllers with clear peering and certificate management.
